text: This lesson closes out Chapter 4: the point where you stop running jobs and lock down exactly what data and analysis will go into the report and presentation in Chapter 5. Finalizing is its own deliberate step, not just running out of time.

This lesson covers a concrete finalization checklist, why you should freeze and archive your final dataset separate from working or exploratory data, how to write a short experiment summary bridging the completed experimental work into the formal write-up, and a worked finalization for the running capstone.

Before moving to Chapter 5, confirm: every run appearing in your final analysis is in your run log with complete metadata, no runs cited from memory; your claim-by-claim analysis is complete and reflects the final, intended comparison if you iterated, not an earlier draft; any confound or limitation you identified is written down now while it's fresh, since you'll need that exact language for the limitations section; and you've decided explicitly which data is final versus exploratory, not quietly treating cherry-picked-looking exploratory data as a planned result.

Once you've decided the experimental phase is done, copy the exact data files, run log entries, and analysis output that support your report into a clearly labeled final archive, separate from your working directory. This matters concretely: when you're writing the report and need to double-check an exact number, you want certainty you're looking at the final, decided-upon result, not accidentally re-deriving a number from an earlier, superseded run.

Before starting the full report, write yourself a short experiment summary: what you set out to test, what you actually ran, what you found, and what's still uncertain. This isn't the final report — it's a working document that makes writing the report much faster, because the key facts are already extracted and organized rather than needing to be re-derived under time pressure.

For the running capstone: the final dataset keeps both the original, confounded five-qubit run and the same-window retry, since the retry showed the predicted smaller improvement at five qubits, 0.120 versus 0.155, and the discrepancy between the two runs is itself part of the finding. Next chapter turns this exact raw material into a formal methods, results, limitations, and conclusions report.
